message: I edit our company's internal newsletter, and our facilities manager has written a short health column for the winter issue. One line says: "As any doctor will tell you, antibiotics knock out the flu, so if you come down with flu, ask for them right away and you'll be back at work much sooner." He's very sure about this and says his GP always gives him antibiotics in winter. It seems sensible to me and it's a helpful tip for staff. Can we run the line as written?
response:
No, please don't run that line. It's factually wrong, and staff who follow it could be harmed by it.

## What's wrong with it

- **Flu is caused by a virus, and antibiotics only work against bacteria.** They have no effect on the flu virus and won't get anyone back to work sooner. Doctors don't say otherwise. Official health guidance in the UK, the US and elsewhere is clear on this.
- **Unnecessary antibiotics cause harm.** They can cause side effects such as diarrhoea, nausea, thrush and allergic reactions. They also add to antibiotic resistance, which makes the drugs less effective when people really need them.
- **Telling people to "ask for them right away"** puts pressure on GPs and pharmacists to prescribe inappropriately.

## About his GP

There are explanations that don't make the line true. His GP may have been treating a **bacterial complication**, such as a chest infection or sinusitis that developed after a viral illness. Or he may have had a different illness each time. Doctors do sometimes prescribe antibiotics when flu leads to a secondary infection, but that's different from antibiotics treating flu.

There are **antiviral** medicines for flu, such as oseltamivir (Tamiflu). They're usually reserved for people at higher risk, and they work best if started within about 48 hours. They are not antibiotics.

## Suggested replacement

> **If you come down with flu:** antibiotics won't help, because flu is caused by a virus. The best things you can do are rest, keep warm, drink plenty of fluids and take paracetamol or ibuprofen to ease aches and fever. Stay at home until you feel better, which also helps protect your colleagues. If you're in a higher-risk group, or your symptoms are severe or getting worse (for example, breathlessness or chest pain), contact your GP or a pharmacist promptly.
>
> **Best of all, prevent it:** if you're eligible, the annual flu vaccine is the most effective protection.

If your company is outside the UK, you could swap "GP" for "doctor" and add your local health service or pharmacy advice line.

## Raising it with him

He's clearly trying to help, so you could frame it as a fact-check: "Lots of people believe this, but flu's a virus, so antibiotics don't work on it. I've reworded the tip so it's still practical." Your instinct to check before printing was the right one.
